title: Transformer Attention
subtitle: Why your LLM slows down as the conversation grows

concepts.name: Autoregressive generation
concepts.description: LLMs write one token at a time, predicting the next token from everything before it.

concepts.name: Tokens
concepts.description: Small chunks of text the model reads as its fundamental units.

concepts.name: Attention
concepts.description: The mechanism that weighs how much each earlier token matters for the next one.

concepts.name: Query / Key / Value
concepts.description: Three roles each token plays when the model compares tokens to each other.

concepts.name: Attention matrix
concepts.description: The full grid of weights between every pair of tokens, recomputed each step.

concepts.name: Multi-head attention
concepts.description: Running several attention patterns in parallel, each hunting a different relationship.

concepts.name: The recompute problem
concepts.description: Each new token re-attends the whole conversation, so cost grows with context.

cards.objective: Create curiosity about why LLMs slow down as context grows.
cards.hook: Why does an LLM slow down as the conversation gets longer?
cards.statement: The first word feels instant. The thousandth one does not. The answer lives inside how the model "thinks" about every word at once.

cards.objective: Plant the central claim: each new token recomputes attention over the whole conversation.

interaction.prompt: Every time the model writes the next word, what does it do with the words it already wrote?

options.label: Remembers its past work
options.explanation: Feels natural — but a plain transformer gets no memory for free.

options.label: Recomputes attention over all of them
options.explanation: Exactly. Each new token re-attends the entire conversation.

options.label: Only looks at the most recent word
options.explanation: Then language would feel like random word salad.

options.label: Frozen after the first token
options.explanation: Then it could only ever write one more word.

cards.reveal: It recomputes. For every new word, the model re-attends every word that came before. That single fact is the story of everything that follows.

cards.objective: Show text entering the model as tokens and the model predicting the next token.
cards.hook: First — the model can't read letters.
cards.statement: Text arrives as tokens, small chunks of words. The model reads the whole sequence at once, then predicts the most likely next token.
cards.footnote: That prediction is the only thing an LLM ever does: guess the next token, over and over.

cards.objective: Show attention as a weighting of earlier tokens when predicting the next token.
cards.hook: But which earlier words should decide the next one?
cards.statement: To choose the next word, the model weighs every earlier word. The ones that matter light up. That weighting — every word versus every word — is attention.

cards.objective: Introduce Q, K, V as the three roles every token plays.
cards.hook: So how does the model decide what "matters"?
cards.statement: For every token, the model builds three representations at once:
cards.footnote: Relevance between two tokens = how strongly one token's Query aligns with another's Key.

cards.objective: Let the learner feel attention weighting by dragging a query toward keys.
cards.hook: Don't take my word for it.
cards.statement: Drag the query toward a word and watch the keys light up. The closer they align, the higher the attention weight.

interactive.title: Drag the Q token
interactive.hint: The closer to a key, the brighter it becomes.

interaction.prompt: Move the query around. What happens to the word that matches?

cards.footnote: Real transformers compute this alignment with a dot product across hundreds of dimensions.

cards.objective: Reveal the full token-by-token attention grid and how it grows.
cards.hook: Now scale it up: every token versus every token.
cards.statement: To write the next word, the model computes a weight between every pair of tokens. That grid is the attention matrix — and it is recomputed fresh at every step.
cards.footnote: Each new token adds an entire row and column to the grid.

cards.objective: Show that transformers run many attention patterns in parallel.
cards.hook: But one attention pattern isn't enough.
cards.statement: A transformer runs this whole comparison in parallel — often 8, 16, or 32 times. Each "head" hunts a different relationship: possession, subject–verb, syntax, distance.
cards.footnote: 8 heads × the same growing grid = the cost multiplies.

cards.objective: Consolidate the central insight through a quick recall test.

interaction.prompt: One more token in. What happens to everything the model already computed?

options.label: It reuses what it already computed
options.explanation: That's exactly what KV Cache does — but a naive transformer doesn't.

options.label: It recomputes Q/K/V for the whole conversation
options.explanation: Yes. Every token re-attends everything — and that's why long chats get slow.

cards.reveal: Every new token recomputes attention for the entire conversation. Long chat → slow chat. That's the problem — and the reason KV Cache exists. But that's a story for another swipe.
